transitiontrees: Transition Trajectories and Dynamics of Variable-Length Pathways or Sequences

Source: R/transitiontrees-package.R
transitiontrees-package.Rd

transitiontrees models how categorical processes unfold: how one state follows another in learning sessions, collaborative work, care pathways or any other ordered record of events. Its model is the variable-order transition tree, known as a prediction suffix tree (Ron, Singer & Tishby, 1996) or variable-length Markov chain (Bühlmann & Wyner, 1999). A first-order Markov chain predicts the next state from the current state alone, and a chain of fixed order \(m\) from the last \(m\) states, with a number of parameters that grows exponentially in \(m\). A transition tree lets the length of the relevant history vary: it keeps a longer context only where the data show that the extra history changes what comes next.

Each node of the tree is a pathway, a run of recent states written from oldest to newest ("A -> B -> C"), with the distribution of the state that followed it. The package treats these pathways as the unit of analysis. It reports which pathways occur, which of them change the prediction relative to a shorter history, how stable they are under resampling, and whether they differ between groups, and it uses the fitted tree to predict, score, simulate and impute sequences. All results are returned as data frames with one row per pathway, sequence or group, and all plots are ggplot2 objects.

Details

With the default floor smoothing, the fitted counts and probabilities match those of the PST package (Gabadinho & Ritschard, 2016). The smoothing schemes other than the floor, the pruning criteria, cross-validated tuning, the bootstrap and the permutation tests are this package's own.

Data input

context_tree() accepts wide sequence tables, lists of sequences, long event logs (reshaped by prepare_input()), and transition network models from tna (Saqr et al., 2025) and Nestimate that carry their sequences. The bundled datasets are trajectories, engagement, group_regulation_long and ai_long.

Fitting and refining a tree

context_tree() fits a tree, or one tree per group. prune_tree() removes contexts that do not change the prediction, smooth_tree() re-estimates probabilities under another smoothing scheme, and compare_pruning() and compare_smoothing() tabulate the alternatives. tune_tree() chooses depth, minimum count, smoothing and pruning by cross-validated perplexity.

Reading pathways

tree_pathways() (also as.data.frame()) lists every pathway; common_pathways(), divergent_pathways() and sharp_pathways() rank them by frequency, divergence from the shorter history, and certainty of the next state. tree_dependence() adds entropies, state_frequencies() gives the state counts, and query_pathway(), pathway_exists(), subtree() and mine_contexts() look up individual pathways.

Fit, prediction and scoring

model_fit() returns log-likelihood, AIC, BIC and perplexity, in-sample or on new data (see also logLik.transitiontrees(), perplexity() and n_nodes()). predict.transitiontrees() predicts the next state, score_sequences(), score_positions() and mine_sequences() score observed sequences, generate_sequences() simulates new ones, and impute_sequences() fills gaps.

Reliability and comparison

bootstrap_pathways() resamples sequences to assess the stability of each pathway. compare_trees() and tree_distance() compare two trees, and compare_groups() tests group differences pathway by pathway with permutation tests.

Visualization

plot.transitiontrees() draws the tree; plot_pathways(), plot_divergence() and plot_distributions() show pathways and their next-state distributions; plot_pruning() shows the pruning decision along one pathway; plot_predictive() shows predictive performance on new data; plot_trajectories() draws the forward tree of sequence beginnings; and plot_difference() and plot_pathway_resamples() show group differences and bootstrap distributions.

References

Bühlmann, P., & Wyner, A. J. (1999). Variable length Markov chains. The Annals of Statistics, 27(2), 480-513. doi:10.1214/aos/1018031204

Gabadinho, A., & Ritschard, G. (2016). Analyzing state sequences with probabilistic suffix trees: The PST R package. Journal of Statistical Software, 72(3). doi:10.18637/jss.v072.i03

Ron, D., Singer, Y., & Tishby, N. (1996). The power of amnesia: Learning probabilistic automata with variable memory length. Machine Learning, 25(2-3), 117-149. doi:10.1023/A:1026490906255

Transition network analysis: A novel framework for modeling, visualizing, and identifying the temporal patterns of learners and learning processes.
